processing: One bud with one opening leaf is spread out, fixed, rolled, then pan-fired in a small wok and a paired wok stage that sets the hooked shape.
harvest_season: Spring, picked mainly at one bud and one opening leaf.
appearance_dry: Tight, hook-curled strips in a fresh jade green.
appearance_wet: Tender shoots opening into small intact clusters.
taste_profile: High, lasting aroma and a mellow, clean, refreshing mouth.

brewing.notes: Typical handling for a pan-fired Zhejiang green: water off the boil, a roomy cup, and pour off before it turns bitter.

vintage_note: Like other Zhejiang greens it is bought as the current year's spring tea and drunk within the year. Earlier, more tender pickings cost more, and grades vary widely between sellers. Check the year on the pack and store it sealed and cool.
description:
Yang Yan Gou Qing is a curled green tea from Yangyan Mountain in Hetou town, northwest of Linhai in Taizhou. The name joins the mountain with gou qing, a word for the hooked green shape, and that shape is the first thing you notice.

The mountain's main peak stands at about 786 metres, and picking is mainly at one bud with one opening leaf. After spreading, fixing and rolling, the leaf goes through two wok stages that tighten it into small hooks.

The cup is described as bright yellow-green, with a high aroma that lasts and a mellow, clean taste. As with similar pan-fired greens, it holds up to slightly hotter water than the most delicate bud teas, though over-steeping still turns it sharp.

The tea is often sold with the local slogan calling it the first gou qing south of the Yangtze, and with comparisons to Long Jing. Take those as sales talk and judge it on its own: tight, even hooks and a clean, lasting smell are what to look for.
history: The tea takes its name from the Yangyan Mountain tea farm in Hetou, and it is named with Panhao among the teas of Linhai. Little is documented about when the style was first made or by whom.
